title: Meeting young Charles Mingus in Los Angeles in 1939
summary: Stewart met teenage Mingus at an L.A. club, admired his plucked solos with several fingers and double stops, though they hardly talked.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Do you recall when you met Charles Mingus?
Yes, I do. I met Charles Mingus out in Los Angeles when I went out there with Slim back in '39.
Oh, he was about 17 then, because he was born in 1922.
Yes, right. That's right.
And he was -- how did you meet him?

I met him at the club out there where he was appearing and of course, Slim and I were working one club and he was working at another club -- I forget the name of the club, but anyway, that's the first time I had met him and it was really a thrill to meet him and hear him play. It was real great.
What was he playing like then, do you recall?

Well, he was doing -- he played good bass and he would execute quite a bit solo-wise, plucking. It was great. At that time, I marveled at his solo work because at that time, I was -- he was plucking while I did my solo work with the bow, of course, and I was wondering how he went about doing the way he -- doing what he did with plucking his solos, you know. He used three or four fingers, which I wasn't used to doing, you know. I did all my work with the bow in my right hand. Of course, I thought it was wonderful.
Was he -- had he started playing those double stops and things?
Yeah.
He was playing them then, was he?
Yes, he was.
Oh, he was, huh?
Yeah.
Yeah, because I didn't know that --
(Playing bass.) You know?
Oh, he was using those kind of things then, was he?
Yes, he was, yes.
Now, Blanton played a few double stops, too, didn't he?
Yes, he did, yes.
Yeah, right. Yeah, so then, like I
know for -- the double stops became -- double and even sometimes triple stops -- became popular like around 1960, you know,
That's right, oh yes.
Then everybody started playing it.
That's right, right. (Playing bass). You know. You know, a hop, skip and a jump, you know?
Uh-huh. And so was he playing into the -- was he also using like the upper registers which he used later in his career at that time? Was he --
Well, at that time, if I remember, he once in a while, he'd get up on top there. (Playing bass.) He'd go up high at times, yes.
Did you and Mingus talk much at that time or did you just kind of meet?
No, we didn't talk too much. Only more or less, I guess you might say, to marvel at the way each other played and what have you.
Was he using the bow much then?
No, not -- I didn't notice that he used the bow hardly at all. He did most of his work pizzicato, you know.
